Caught In Cambodia's Surrogacy Crackdown

By: Chwayitisa Futshane | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
... Escaping the crackdown with a pregnant surrogate

Unique Selling Point:
Dateline meets the Australian parents who risked it all to build a family through overseas surrogacy. We investigate how Cambodia’s crackdown left women raising children they never wanted.

Script:



VISUALS AUDIO
PTT

Suburban Australia
- Kids






Family videos

Hectic Cambodia GVs





Xu in jail
For many Australians, creating a family is a life dream

But for those unable to have children, it can be out of reach

Anthony: I thought as a gay man… : I just thought it was kind of a pipe dream. I never thought it could happen.

SURROGACY IN SOUTH EAST ASIA WAS ONCE A LIFELINE FOR PEOPLE WHO COULD not CONCEIVE

BUT IT DIDN’T END HAPPILY FOR EVERYONE INVOLVED

Daneth
I still remember the image of the police arresting me.
While I was delivering the baby, shackles were put on my legs even though I was pregnant.


DESPITE SURROGACY CRACKDOWNS - the demand for a woman’s womb is unwavering

LEAVING MANY SOUTH EAST ASIAN WOMEN VULNERABLE

Sopheara:
Before some foreigners came here for the women to have the baby. Now they take women to have a baby in another country.
What makes a rightful parent and what would you risk to become one?

TITLE: CAMBODIA’S SURROGACY CRACKDOWN
PERTH




SUBURBAN NEIGHBOURHOOD / HOUSE EXTERIORS





KIDS getting ready
UPSOT
-----Chaos in the house, Iris playing ‘Bop It’-----

IT’S SATURDAY MORNING IN PERTH


THE KIDS ARE UP EARLY

AND DAD’S ANTHONY AND JOSEPH ARE GETTING READY FOR WEEKEND SPORT



7 year old IRIS IS THE SOCCER PLAYER IN THE FAMILY

WHILST TWIN BROTHER JULIAN LIKES BOOKS and ballet

OLDER SISTER CELESTE WHO’S 9 is the artist











But for a long time, this family was just a fantasy

Anthony:
I didn't think I could have kids. I thought as a gay man, man, there wasn't much of an opportunity for me to have children.

Anthony:
And it wasn't until I met Joseph and we got talking and we talked about kids and just thought it was kind of a pipe dream. I never thought it could happen.
VO
Their journey to actually creating a family was… unorthodox.
Joseph:
We did all the research. We went to speak to a lawyer and just ask for options and I wanted to adopt, but it just wasn't viable. I wasn't willing to wait six or seven years to have a child. So we went down the path of surrogacy.
What did your family and friends think? Were they like.. “Great. Go for it”? Or what was the conversation?
Joseph:
My family was a bit shocked at first.
Anthony:
There was one example where we were told not to go to a family event with our new baby because it was going to be embarrassing.
VO
But coming up against family was just the first hurdle to having a baby…

GFX map - highlighting relevant states

Baby blanket -- quilted map

No surrogacy overseas:
ACT
NSW
QLD Australia has a patchwork of surrogacy laws
Commercial surrogacy - where someone is PAID to carry a baby - is illegal across Australia
Some states even prohibit engaging in commercial surrogacy overseas
Altruistic surrogacy -- where a surrogate makes no profit… is legal
But in Western Australia… Anthony and Joseph still faced barriers


Anthony:
So altruistic surrogacy is legal in Western Australia for straight couples, straight women, lesbian couples, but not gay men. So we're the only ones that can't go through that process.

VO
Their only option to pursue surrogacy was to go abroad
And in 2014, they chose Thailand
From there, it was about choosing a surrogate
Anthony and Joseph IV Anthony:
They call them tummy mummies. There are many surrogates, there were many surrogates that were available, very- seemed very professionals that go through all the details about who they were, their backgrounds
VO
Joseph’s sister was the egg donor


And Anthony… THE BIOLOGICAL FATHER

Anthony:
Well I went over to do my bit. It all seemed very, I don't know, very safe.
VO
Within a matter of weeks, they got the news they’d been hoping for

They were pregnant



Joseph:
Over the moon. So happy.
Anthony:
Every week we’d get an update with a little… how it was growing and the heartbeat. And it was just like we'd wait for that email. It was a great time.
And that was before Baby Gammy hit the news
THIRD PARTY FILE

THAILAND SURROGACY SHUTDOWN
TV NEWS PRESENTER upsot:
Now to a story sparking international headlines, an Australian couple refused to take home their baby from a surrogate mother because the infant had down syndrome

Anthony: it changed everything in Thailand.

TV NEWS PRESENTER 2 UPSOT:
Thailand’s made its first move to ban commercial surrogacies in the wake of the baby Gammy scandal.











Anthony:
So the police had shut down the agency, the doctor was arrested, we couldn't get through to anyone.
And we were so worried. Our baby’s in the womb of this woman only 4 months into pregnancy and we were so worried something might happen - something untoward might happen.
We couldn't believe someone in Australia, in Western Australia had done this to their child and abandoned a child over in Thailand, basically ruined it for everyone.
VO

Joseph and Anthony got Celeste out under an amnesty for surrogate babies already in the womb

But, they faced judgement along the way


Anthony:
I guess people asked us hard questions and it made us think about what we were doing. But we had put so much thought into this anyway. It wasn't something that you can just turn around and do.

But once the stress had simmered down


ALT
And their wider family had fallen in love with baby Celeste -- welcoming her with open arms --


They questioned if their family was truly complete


Joseph:
I still was feeling clucky. I've always wanted Celeste to have siblings to play with.
Joseph: I was willing to try again and risk it basically.

Anthony:
I thought you were mad. I thought you were crazy after the experience we went through in Thailand, to go trhough the same thing again, in even a more third world country I guess…

VO
Sure enough -- as one door closed, another opened

A new industry was booming… just across the border
CAMBODIA INTRO
CHAOTIC STREET TRAFFIC




DRIVING SHOTS


TEXT ON SCREEN: PHNOM PENH, CAMBODIA

PTC

I’ve come to CAMBODIA to find out how people here have helped foreigners build families, and I’m heading to the outskirts of Phnom Penh to meet with one woman who used to be a surrogate.

After Thailand cracked down on surrogacy, many Australians turned to Cambodia in search of a new ‘tummy mummy’

The industry here WAS legal, but relied on women in lower income areas...

Like here...

DANETH


One woman, Daneth was working in a garment factory in 2017 when she was approached by a colleague


They told us that they have a place where they needed surrogate mothers.

Rhiona: How did you feel about carrying a baby for someone else?

Daneth: At that time, I was wondering. Why do they not look for wives? Why do they need surrogate mothers? Or do they sell the baby? I asked them that, but they said ‘no’ it was not like that.

I asked if we’d be arrested for being surrogate mothers. They said it’d be fine. They’d been doing it for a long time. And had never had any problems. The parents came to take the babies legally, so I stopped asking questions.

VO
Daneth was told she would be carrying for a Chinese man who used a Russian donor egg

She was also told she would be paid a stipend each month

And get 9 THOUSAND US DOLLARS
once the baby was delivered

I thought the compensation was acceptable, I had already had a baby, so I thought it was fine.

But the road to that reward would be more difficult than Daneth anticipated…

Once I was pregnant, my health checkups were all positive, then I had to live in the villa.

VO
Daneth was forced to stay in a house with around 30 other surrogates for the duration of her pregnancy

The agency running the house only allowed her to leave for brief periods

She says they kept a close eye on the women for health reasons

If the foetus didn’t develop properly, they’d ask us to have an abortion. The baby had to develop well or they’d end the pregnancy. If the pregnancy ended, we were finished with them.

VO
Hearing little of the outside world, Daneth had no idea that what she was doing would soon be treated as a crime

PHOTOS:





3RD PARTY FILE (CAMBODIA SURROGACY SHUTDOWN) She was 8 months pregnant when the villa was raided by police


Cambodia had cracked down on surrogacy and made examples of those who were caught in the crossfire

Q: How did you feel when the police came through the door?

We were crying because we were scared. We did not know what to do. They threatened and shouted at us. We were frightened to tears. Everyone was pregnant.
VO
Daneth and the other surrogates were arrested under the notion that surrogacy is a form of human trafficking

They were then held in this military hospital until they were ready to deliver

While I was delivering the baby, they shackled my legs to the corner of the bed. I felt terrible.

Daneth scrolling through baby photos VO
It was a traumatic birth


Before he was born, I did not like him. I got angry with him and questioned why I was there.

After I delivered him though, I felt that those thoughts disappeared. I loved him. I did not know how it happened because I already had a baby, but it was a completely different love.

Anger and hatred are all gone, and only love remains.
That was the first time Daneth saw the baby

But not the last

Her looming CRIMINAL charges were dropped on an extraordinary condition

The court allowed me to be released from custody, but I’d have to raise the baby by myself.

VO
Daneth agreed to the terms

And inspired by his biological father.... she named the boy… China

BATHING CHINA
INTRO CHINA

Close your eyes
Take your hands away
Rub your arms

SLAPS HIS FACE

Don’t slap your face.

I’m choking!
take your hands away
No it’s going inside my nose
Take it away
it’s going to go inside my nose




VISION OF BOYS DOING HOMEWORK TOGETHER WITH DANETH




VO
Daneth never received the money she was promised
Instead, she was left to raise a stranger’s child
Along with her biological son
HOMEWORK SCENE

MUM: Where are your colouring pencils?

- Let’s write “1” for mummy please. Write “one” for me baby.
- Come on clever boy.
- How do I write “six”?
- Like this.

Rhi Q: I can see you’re doing homework with him. What’s the hardest part of raising him on your own?
Answer: The hardest part is education. He is too stubborn. He doesn’t listen to us much. That’s the hardest part.

- Yes I know!
- Very clever, my boy!
- Wrong again
- You can erase it

RHI Q: He looks differrent to your other son Do people make comments?
Daneth: People say that he looks different because he is not Cambodian child


People tease him. I ask them not to. I beg them to have pity on me, but they say if I do not want to hear such rumours I should’nt live here.

VO
Daneth feels like the window for telling China about his background is slowly closing

At this point, I don’t know what to say to make everyone happy. I think if I tell him a lie, he will learn the truth one day.

VO
In the meantime, Daneth says she’s seen Chinese people around the neighbourhood– she thinks they could be extended family who’ve come to see what the boy looks like

A reminder of another life he could have lived

And his biological father who lives without him
XU
PRISON EXTERIORS

FOOTAGE OF PRISON WAGON The intended parent was a Chinese man named Xu Wenjun

He came to meet his biological son, but shortly after this photo was taken

He was arrested on human trafficking charges for attempting to take him back to China

He was sentenced to 15 years in Cambodian prison


VO
The story of Daneth and Wenjun is a sliding door moment for AUSTRALIAN COUPLE Anthony and Joseph

They were pregnant with twins at the time of the
Cambodian crackdown

BACK TO PERTH
Rhiona: One of the more extreme measures that the Cambodian government took during the ban was arresting some of the surrogates and then suspending their jail sentences on the condition that they raise the kids themselves. How does it feel hearing that?
Joseph:
Wow, I did not know there were any cases of that… yes, surrogates or even intended parents would get arrested. But this is southeast Asia. Normally you can sort of wiggle your way out.
Anthony: Influence people.
Joseph: Yeah, exactly.
Anthony: I didn't think that they'd be in that situation. To me, that's insane.

Anthony:
And now to be responsible for someone that's not their biological child for the rest of their lives is just, I don't know how anyone can do that to me is cruel, extremely cruel. Both to the surrogate mother and to the parents overseas, but also of course to the kid
I just imagine Iris and Julian now in Cambodia.
VO
Anthony and Joseph only narrowly escaped Cambodia’s crackdown.
On advice from their agent, they chose to smuggle their surrogate out of Cambodia
While Thailand had outlawed surrogacy for locals, she was able to give birth there - as a foreigner
ALT


Anthony:
We had to do this in the middle of the night. She had to go over to Thailand at a place that doesn't have a border crossing into the north of Thailand, into the jungle from Cambodia.

Joseph:
Flying wasn't an option. So there were reports of officials boarding the plane and basically arresting some of the surrogates.
Anthony:
There were a lot of sleepless nights thinking about it and ensuring that this was the right thing and there weren't many other options for us. I would have wanted it to be different. It’s not ideal and its not fun being thousands of km away unable to communicate with her and assure her that we were doing this for all the right reasons and that we’re gonna look after her. That was tough, it was really tough.
CHAB DAI
VO
Almost a decade on from the crackdown, there are no specific laws against surrogacy in Cambodia

The government still uses human trafficking laws to enforce the ban

Hearing just how far people will go to build a family, I want to know if the ban really brought numbers down

Or if it simply changed the game



Sopheara -- from local NGO Chab Dai -- works directly with survivors of human trafficking

Rhiona:
Do you think that the Cambodia’s surrogacy ban was effective crackdown was effective, that it helped keep women safe?
Sopheara:
More or less it can help, but the brokers and buyers
Still find some other ways to trick.
For example, if they work in the garment factory, a person approaches and persuades you that if you go to China you will get this salary and you can return home whenever you want.
But they end up just providing sex services to the Chinese family.
GFX
Stitches travelling to china



China is the main country Cambodian women are trafficked to


It’s long-standing one child policy led to a shortage of women in the country

As parents favoured a boy to continue the family line

As a result, the practice of bride trafficking from across the region has been steadily increasing as more men come of age

Sopheara IV But Sopheara tells me there’s more to it…

Most cases of forced marriage he sees are driven by the desire for children

Sopheara:
Before some foreigners came here for women to have the baby. Now they take women to have babies in another country.
COMING UP

I meet a woman trafficked to China to provide children for a stranger…

I think he did not consider me as his wife. He just wanted to have a baby.

AD BREAK
Moody driving shots


VO
I’m in Cambodia to find out whether the government’s crackdown on surrogacy made some women more vulnerable to being trafficked abroad

NIGHT COMMS

VO
A local NGO is connecting me with a survivor

But we have to be discreet

The Cambodian government can be sensitive to the coverage of human trafficking cases



GFX TEXT MSG:
Sopheara
We just want to mitigate the risk…


GFX TEXT MSG: We can meet each other at this place and then head to the survivor’s home.

TAKEO PROVINCE
Driving to Takeo (following their car)

Drone

Arriving in Takeo

Shots of neighbourhood

SURVIVOR








Walking shots
VO
Alt: For her safety, we’ve also agreed to keep the survivors identity hidden
We’ll call her Chan
Wides of the area Chan was working in a garment factory, much like Daneth, when she was approached with an enticing offer

My friend asked me if I’d work in China. She said she’d get me work there for 3 months so I could get money like others who’d gone before. So, I followed them
VO
Chan was just 18 years old when she agreed to go
RECON SCENE They took us out one night and took us to a guesthouse. We stayed there for a night. The next morning, someone picked me up from the guest house to go to Vietnam.
I was told not to talk.




I felt scared.
I vomited the whole way. No one looked after me.


VO
It was only on arrival in China, after being locked in a room, that Chan realised she had been trafficked

They asked me to dress up, do make up and take some photos to show to Chinese people.

VO
A Cambodian woman told her she was here to marry a Chinese man

I was crying and she told me not to. I was afraid they would abuse me.
VO
After travelling another 5 hours, Chan met her new husband

Rhiona: How did he treat you?

He was violent,
He wanted me to sleep with him

So, I used hand gestures to tell him to kill me.
I don't think he considered me as his wife. He just wanted to have a baby.

Q: How were you feeling at that time?

I felt that once they sell you, they never let you go back to Cambodia. He told me if I had a baby, he’d let me go back to Cambodia. And I agreed.



When I was pregnant, I felt worried. I’d never had a baby or a husband before. I did not know how painful the delivery would be. I was really scared.

VO
Chan gave birth at a local hospital

(pause)
But for her captor - one child wasn’t enough...


After I delivered the baby, my Chinese husband wanted me to have another within a few months

They wouldn’t let me go out, I was confined to the house.
VO
It would be another 4 years until Chan was able to make contact with someone back home
And when she was finally able to escape – she had to leave her two children behind in China
Chan’s story is harrowing…
And not an isolated incident
ALT.

After years of climbing case numbers, the US State Department has branded Cambodia with the worst possible trafficking rating

Despite a crackdown on surrogacy claiming to curb it


We contacted the Cambodian government official who led the crackdown, and who’s responsible for anti-trafficking initiatives - CHOU BUN ENG but she declined an interview.


For parents like Anthony and Joseph, the links drawn between surrogacy and human trafficking are extremely confronting

PERTH



















































KIDS PLAYING



Q: How does it feel hearing a word like that be associated with the process you went through?

Joseph:
It's a dirty word. I don't want to be associated with it. And it's devastating just to try and link the two.
Anthony:
It’s not accurate. At the end of the day, we had a family, it's not accurate to call it human trafficking. It's about giving people who can’t have kids an opportunity to have children. It’s something that happens in Australia. Women do this, the amazing women who give up their womb and have children for other people without any financial return.
VO
But pursuing surrogacy overseas came with a hefty price tag
Anthony: For the three children we spent around 200,000 Australian dollars…

Did you think that this was a mutually beneficial deal, that it was win-win for you and the surrogate?

Joseph:
Definitely works for us, but I didn't want to know about the other end. What do you mean? As in I know they'll probably get a less amount, obviously part of the deal, most of the money would definitely go to the agency.
Anthony and Joseph tried to balance the scales FOR THEIR SURROGATE
Joseph:
a couple of days before we were leaving, just to say final goodbyes, Anthony took her to Chinatown in Bangkok to buy some gold. Gold can't go wrong with there. And…
Anthony: Look, it was fraught, we just wanted to make sure that we were doing the right thing. We had two kids, that’s an amazing gift for us and we just wanted to make sure that she was rewarded…
Joseph:
And a bit of time with the twins as well. Yeah, so we gave her alone time with the twins to say goodbyes and we still keep in touch on Facebook, send her photos here and there.
Q: Knowing what you know now, copping some criticism, going through multiple crackdowns… Was it worth it?
Anthony:
Of course. Of course. It's worth it. It's absolutely worth it. We have three beautiful children and I just feel so blessed that we were able to do this in a way that I feel completely confident in and I'm so happy with the results.
It was a journey and you wonder if you made missteps, but at the end of the day you did the best that you could. And I think every parent does that.
They want to make sure they do the best, not just for their kids, but make sure they have the kids in the right way.

Anthony and Joseph are lobbying to make surrogacy accessible for gay men in Western Australia
To help others like them fulfil their dream of a family

Joseph:
Surrogacy isn't say unnatural. In the end, we still want a family. We still want to provide shelter, love support for the child. It's no different having a child the other way.

I asked them that, but they said ‘no’ it was not like that. I asked if we’d be arrested for being surrogate mothers. They said it’d be fine. They’d been doing it for a long time. And had never had any problems. The parents came to take the babies legally, so I stopped asking questions. VO Daneth was told she would be carrying for a Chinese man who used a Russian donor egg She was also told she would be paid a stipend each month And get 9 THOUSAND US DOLLARS once the baby was delivered I thought the compensation was acceptable, I had already had a baby, so I thought it was fine. But the road to that reward would be more difficult than Daneth anticipated… Once I was pregnant, my health checkups were all positive, then I had to live in the villa. VO Daneth was forced to stay in a house with around 30 other surrogates for the duration of her pregnancy The agency running the house only allowed her to leave for brief periods She says they kept a close eye on the women for health reasons If the foetus didn’t develop properly, they’d ask us to have an abortion. The baby had to develop well or they’d end the pregnancy. If the pregnancy ended, we were finished with them. VO Hearing little of the outside world, Daneth had no idea that what she was doing would soon be treated as a crime PHOTOS: 3RD PARTY FILE (CAMBODIA SURROGACY SHUTDOWN) She was 8 months pregnant when the villa was raided by police Cambodia had cracked down on surrogacy and made examples of those who were caught in the crossfire Q: How did you feel when the police came through the door? We were crying because we were scared. We did not know what to do. They threatened and shouted at us. We were frightened to tears. Everyone was pregnant. VO Daneth and the other surrogates were arrested under the notion that surrogacy is a form of human trafficking They were then held in this military hospital until they were ready to deliver While I was delivering the baby, they shackled my legs to the corner of the bed. I felt terrible. Daneth scrolling through baby photos VO It was a traumatic birth Before he was born, I did not like him. I got angry with him and questioned why I was there. After I delivered him though, I felt that those thoughts disappeared. I loved him. I did not know how it happened because I already had a baby, but it was a completely different love. Anger and hatred are all gone, and only love remains. That was the first time Daneth saw the baby But not the last Her looming CRIMINAL charges were dropped on an extraordinary condition The court allowed me to be released from custody, but I’d have to raise the baby by myself. VO Daneth agreed to the terms And inspired by his biological father.... she named the boy… China BATHING CHINA INTRO CHINA Close your eyes Take your hands away Rub your arms SLAPS HIS FACE Don’t slap your face. I’m choking! take your hands away No it’s going inside my nose Take it away it’s going to go inside my nose VISION OF BOYS DOING HOMEWORK TOGETHER WITH DANETH VO Daneth never received the money she was promised Instead, she was left to raise a stranger’s child Along with her biological son HOMEWORK SCENE MUM: Where are your colouring pencils? - Let’s write “1” for mummy please. Write “one” for me baby. - Come on clever boy. - How do I write “six”? - Like this. Rhi Q: I can see you’re doing homework with him. What’s the hardest part of raising him on your own? Answer: The hardest part is education. He is too stubborn. He doesn’t listen to us much. That’s the hardest part. - Yes I know! - Very clever, my boy! - Wrong again - You can erase it RHI Q: He looks differrent to your other son Do people make comments? Daneth: People say that he looks different because he is not Cambodian child People tease him. I ask them not to. I beg them to have pity on me, but they say if I do not want to hear such rumours I should’nt live here. VO Daneth feels like the window for telling China about his background is slowly closing At this point, I don’t know what to say to make everyone happy. I think if I tell him a lie, he will learn the truth one day. VO In the meantime, Daneth says she’s seen Chinese people around the neighbourhood– she thinks they could be extended family who’ve come to see what the boy looks like A reminder of another life he could have lived And his biological father who lives without him XU PRISON EXTERIORS FOOTAGE OF PRISON WAGON The intended parent was a Chinese man named Xu Wenjun He came to meet his biological son, but shortly after this photo was taken He was arrested on human trafficking charges for attempting to take him back to China He was sentenced to 15 years in Cambodian prison VO The story of Daneth and Wenjun is a sliding door moment for AUSTRALIAN COUPLE Anthony and Joseph They were pregnant with twins at the time of the Cambodian crackdown BACK TO PERTH Rhiona: One of the more extreme measures that the Cambodian government took during the ban was arresting some of the surrogates and then suspending their jail sentences on the condition that they raise the kids themselves. How does it feel hearing that? Joseph: Wow, I did not know there were any cases of that… yes, surrogates or even intended parents would get arrested. But this is southeast Asia. Normally you can sort of wiggle your way out. Anthony: Influence people. Joseph: Yeah, exactly. Anthony: I didn't think that they'd be in that situation. To me, that's insane. Anthony: And now to be responsible for someone that's not their biological child for the rest of their lives is just, I don't know how anyone can do that to me is cruel, extremely cruel. Both to the surrogate mother and to the parents overseas, but also of course to the kid I just imagine Iris and Julian now in Cambodia. VO Anthony and Joseph only narrowly escaped Cambodia’s crackdown. On advice from their agent, they chose to smuggle their surrogate out of Cambodia While Thailand had outlawed surrogacy for locals, she was able to give birth there - as a foreigner ALT Anthony: We had to do this in the middle of the night. She had to go over to Thailand at a place that doesn't have a border crossing into the north of Thailand, into the jungle from Cambodia. Joseph: Flying wasn't an option. So there were reports of officials boarding the plane and basically arresting some of the surrogates. Anthony: There were a lot of sleepless nights thinking about it and ensuring that this was the right thing and there weren't many other options for us. I would have wanted it to be different. It’s not ideal and its not fun being thousands of km away unable to communicate with her and assure her that we were doing this for all the right reasons and that we’re gonna look after her. That was tough, it was really tough. CHAB DAI VO Almost a decade on from the crackdown, there are no specific laws against surrogacy in Cambodia The government still uses human trafficking laws to enforce the ban Hearing just how far people will go to build a family, I want to know if the ban really brought numbers down Or if it simply changed the game Sopheara -- from local NGO Chab Dai -- works directly with survivors of human trafficking Rhiona: Do you think that the Cambodia’s surrogacy ban was effective crackdown was effective, that it helped keep women safe? Sopheara: More or less it can help, but the brokers and buyers Still find some other ways to trick. For example, if they work in the garment factory, a person approaches and persuades you that if you go to China you will get this salary and you can return home whenever you want. But they end up just providing sex services to the Chinese family. GFX Stitches travelling to china China is the main country Cambodian women are trafficked to It’s long-standing one child policy led to a shortage of women in the country As parents favoured a boy to continue the family line As a result, the practice of bride trafficking from across the region has been steadily increasing as more men come of age Sopheara IV But Sopheara tells me there’s more to it… Most cases of forced marriage he sees are driven by the desire for children Sopheara: Before some foreigners came here for women to have the baby. Now they take women to have babies in another country. COMING UP I meet a woman trafficked to China to provide children for a stranger… I think he did not consider me as his wife. He just wanted to have a baby. AD BREAK Moody driving shots VO I’m in Cambodia to find out whether the government’s crackdown on surrogacy made some women more vulnerable to being trafficked abroad NIGHT COMMS VO A local NGO is connecting me with a survivor But we have to be discreet The Cambodian government can be sensitive to the coverage of human trafficking cases GFX TEXT MSG: Sopheara We just want to mitigate the risk… GFX TEXT MSG: We can meet each other at this place and then head to the survivor’s home. TAKEO PROVINCE Driving to Takeo (following their car) Drone Arriving in Takeo Shots of neighbourhood SURVIVOR Walking shots VO Alt: For her safety, we’ve also agreed to keep the survivors identity hidden We’ll call her Chan Wides of the area Chan was working in a garment factory, much like Daneth, when she was approached with an enticing offer My friend asked me if I’d work in China. She said she’d get me work there for 3 months so I could get money like others who’d gone before. So, I followed them VO Chan was just 18 years old when she agreed to go RECON SCENE They took us out one night and took us to a guesthouse. We stayed there for a night. The next morning, someone picked me up from the guest house to go to Vietnam. I was told not to talk. I felt scared. I vomited the whole way. No one looked after me. VO It was only on arrival in China, after being locked in a room, that Chan realised she had been trafficked They asked me to dress up, do make up and take some photos to show to Chinese people. VO A Cambodian woman told her she was here to marry a Chinese man I was crying and she told me not to. I was afraid they would abuse me. VO After travelling another 5 hours, Chan met her new husband Rhiona: How did he treat you? He was violent, He wanted me to sleep with him So, I used hand gestures to tell him to kill me. I don't think he considered me as his wife. He just wanted to have a baby. Q: How were you feeling at that time? I felt that once they sell you, they never let you go back to Cambodia. He told me if I had a baby, he’d let me go back to Cambodia. And I agreed. When I was pregnant, I felt worried. I’d never had a baby or a husband before. I did not know how painful the delivery would be. I was really scared. VO Chan gave birth at a local hospital (pause) But for her captor - one child wasn’t enough... After I delivered the baby, my Chinese husband wanted me to have another within a few months They wouldn’t let me go out, I was confined to the house. VO It would be another 4 years until Chan was able to make contact with someone back home And when she was finally able to escape – she had to leave her two children behind in China Chan’s story is harrowing… And not an isolated incident ALT. After years of climbing case numbers, the US State Department has branded Cambodia with the worst possible trafficking rating Despite a crackdown on surrogacy claiming to curb it We contacted the Cambodian government official who led the crackdown, and who’s responsible for anti-trafficking initiatives - CHOU BUN ENG but she declined an interview. For parents like Anthony and Joseph, the links drawn between surrogacy and human trafficking are extremely confronting PERTH KIDS PLAYING Q: How does it feel hearing a word like that be associated with the process you went through? Joseph: It's a dirty word. I don't want to be associated with it. And it's devastating just to try and link the two. Anthony: It’s not accurate. At the end of the day, we had a family, it's not accurate to call it human trafficking. It's about giving people who can’t have kids an opportunity to have children. It’s something that happens in Australia. Women do this, the amazing women who give up their womb and have children for other people without any financial return. VO But pursuing surrogacy overseas came with a hefty price tag Anthony: For the three children we spent around 200,000 Australian dollars… Did you think that this was a mutually beneficial deal, that it was win-win for you and the surrogate? Joseph: Definitely works for us, but I didn't want to know about the other end. What do you mean? As in I know they'll probably get a less amount, obviously part of the deal, most of the money would definitely go to the agency. Anthony and Joseph tried to balance the scales FOR THEIR SURROGATE Joseph: a couple of days before we were leaving, just to say final goodbyes, Anthony took her to Chinatown in Bangkok to buy some gold. Gold can't go wrong with there. And… Anthony: Look, it was fraught, we just wanted to make sure that we were doing the right thing. We had two kids, that’s an amazing gift for us and we just wanted to make sure that she was rewarded… Joseph: And a bit of time with the twins as well. Yeah, so we gave her alone time with the twins to say goodbyes and we still keep in touch on Facebook, send her photos here and there. Q: Knowing what you know now, copping some criticism, going through multiple crackdowns… Was it worth it? Anthony: Of course. Of course. It's worth it. It's absolutely worth it. We have three beautiful children and I just feel so blessed that we were able to do this in a way that I feel completely confident in and I'm so happy with the results. It was a journey and you wonder if you made missteps, but at the end of the day you did the best that you could. And I think every parent does that. They want to make sure they do the best, not just for their kids, but make sure they have the kids in the right way. Anthony and Joseph are lobbying to make surrogacy accessible for gay men in Western Australia To help others like them fulfil their dream of a family Joseph: Surrogacy isn't say unnatural. In the end, we still want a family. We still want to provide shelter, love support for the child. It's no different having a child the other way.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Dateline meets the Australian parents who risked it all to build a family through overseas surrogacy. We investigate how Cambodia’s crackdown left women raising children they never wanted.
